Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Expectation2: Leading the daily prayers in the mosque
Situation2: The regular backup is away, so most congregants expect him to step forward for the scheduled prayer.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was preparing to leave for the mosque. It was Samir, his voice trembling, telling me his car had broken down on the highway. He was alone, scared, and needed me to come get him right away. My heart raced—I knew how much he relied on me, especially in moments like this. But tonight, the backup imam was out of town, and everyone at the mosque was expecting me to lead the prayer. I could already picture the congregation gathering, waiting for me to step forward, their trust in me unwavering. I felt the weight of their expectations pressing down on me, the sacred responsibility I carried as their imam. At the same time, I couldn’t ignore Samir’s desperation; he was my friend, and friends are supposed to be there in emergencies. The clock ticked, my mind spinning between the pull of duty and the call of friendship, both urgent, both impossible to ignore.
